entry.evidence: Since global positioning with satellite systems is not possible in subsurface environments, the data recorded by these platforms are not spatially referenced.

sequences.source_document: Publisher XML full text (jats_text) with PDF for figures

steps.action: Authors pose the need for sensing methods that retrieve water pressure and flow paths of glacial drainage over relevant spatial scales, since existing pressure data are indirect or point scale.
steps.quote: developing sensing methods that retrieve drainage parameters (e.g., water pressure, water flow paths) over problem-relevant spatial scales is critical

steps.action: Authors rely on their earlier demonstration that IMU and pressure signals from submersible drifters repeat across deployments in a supraglacial channel.
steps.quote: [...] of measurements from inertial measurement units (IMUs), alongside pressure recordings in a supraglacial channel, has been demonstrated

steps.action: Authors adopt the mobile-robotics approach to dead-reckoning error: probabilistic mapping with salient features used as landmarks.
steps.quote: In mobile robotics, this problem is often addressed using probabilistic mapping algorithms

steps.action: Authors use their previously built submersible drifter (pressure sensors plus 9-DOF IMU) and GNSS surface drifter (Tuhtan et al. 2020) as measurement and reference platforms.
steps.quote: A detailed description of the submersible drifter can be found in

steps.action: Authors design the test: validate the reconstruction first on a supraglacial channel against a GNSS reference, then apply it to the englacial channel with GNSS 2020, satellite and 1999 GPR references (Table 1).
steps.quote: In order to test and validate our reconstruction algorithms, both drifter platforms were deployed in the small supraglacial channel

steps.action: Field deployments in July 2019: 18 submersible-drifter deployments in the supraglacial and 16 in the englacial channel, a GNSS-drifter revisit of the melted-out channel in August 2020, and digitizing of the canyon and river from Planet imagery.
steps.quote: Both platforms were then deployed into the englacial channel via a former moulin

steps.action: Authors build the reconstruction pipeline: changepoint segmentation, Savitzky-Golay filtering, outlier removal, mean correction and NED rotation; then iHMM feature extraction with beam sampling, piecewise double integration between features, declination correction, two-point rescaling and dynamic-time-warping averaging.
steps.quote: a more computationally expensive but more flexible infinite hidden Markov model (iHMM) will be used to address these limitations

steps.action: Authors reconstruct the supraglacial flow path from 11 complete drifter datasets.
steps.quote: The reconstruction was based on 11 submersible-drifter deployments.

steps.action: Authors compare the reconstruction with the averaged 26-track GNSS reference: mean position error 3.9 m (range 2.0-11.1 m) and length overestimate of 6.5 %.
steps.quote: [...] a water flow path, which is on average within 3.9 m of [...] channel

steps.action: Authors vary the number of deployments averaged and show that the average error converges after six datasets (Fig. 6).
steps.quote: the average position error from our reconstruction converges after six datasets

steps.action: Authors map the spatially referenced pressure distribution along the supraglacial channel.
steps.quote: The resulting pressure distribution map shows the pressure variations along the channel

steps.action: Authors reconstruct the englacial flow path from six complete datasets.
steps.quote: The reconstruction from the IMU data, collected in 2019 (six datasets), leads to the mean water flow path

steps.action: Authors compare the englacial reconstruction with the 2020 GNSS track and the satellite-derived river: average errors of 12.1 m overall, 13.3 m in the channel and 10.9 m in the canyon and river; modelled length 1027 m.
steps.quote: The englacial channel part of the reconstruction has an average position error of 13.3 m compared to the 2020 GNSS reference

steps.action: Authors map the englacial pressure distribution (mean 1011.7 hPa, SD 3.4 hPa) and find one high-pressure zone before the canyon exit.
steps.quote: reveals one zone of higher pressure shortly before the englacial channel exits into the open canyon

steps.action: Authors qualitatively compare the track shape with the 1999 GPR map of Stuart et al. (2003) and match the river turn on satellite imagery (Fig. 7b).
steps.quote: shows good accordance in the overall shape of the water flow path

steps.action: Authors attribute part of the supraglacial error to the limited accuracy of the GNSS reference (±3 m static, worse in turbulence, oversmoothed by averaging), not to the method.
steps.quote: An average error of 3.9 m for the reconstruction versus the GNSS reference is therefore likely below the accuracy of the GNSS reference track itself.

steps.action: After the englacial length mismatch (1027 m vs 835 m), authors add an 85 m missing section from handheld GPS and revise the length error to 107 m (11.6 %); they note that the satellite reference underestimates length and that drifter eddying overestimates it.
steps.quote: This leaves a difference of 107 m between reference water flow path length and the reconstruction

steps.action: Authors state two rivals for discrepancies with earlier studies, reconstruction inaccuracy or channel evolution, and leave them unresolved.
steps.quote: It is therefore difficult to establish if the discrepancies between our reconstruction and previous studies are due to an inaccurate reconstruction

steps.action: Authors compare pressure regime and variability with Stuart et al. (2003), who found pressurized flow, and with their earlier drifter work: flow is now atmospheric and the SD is similar to earlier data.
steps.quote: The pressures recorded by the submersible drifters in the englacial channel show flow under atmospheric conditions.

steps.action: Authors interpret the englacial high-pressure zone as a step-pool sequence with a large step riser.
steps.quote: we interpret this as the presence of a step-pool sequence with a large step riser

steps.action: Authors check the interpretation against 2018 speleological observation of a 2.5 m step riser at the same location and against lidar scans (Kamintzis et al. 2019).
steps.quote: [...] confirmed by speleological investigations in 2018, where a roughly 2.5 m high step riser was found at the same location.

steps.action: Authors keep the claim that the method can identify and locate step-pool sequences.
steps.quote: This shows that our method allows for identifying and locating step-pool sequences within glacial channels.

steps.action: Authors estimate single-deployment precision (0.66 %, using Eq. 4 of Alexander et al. 2020a) and, from recovery and utility rates, that at least three deployments are needed for a 1 km channel.
steps.quote: leads to a precision of 0.66 % with just one deployment

steps.action: Authors compare their length errors with the GPR result of Church et al. (2020) and argue that the error scales with channel length.
steps.quote: This indicates that the error in our method scales with the length of the investigated channel

steps.action: Authors restrict the claim to planar topology: no 3D (gravity vector not corrected), no channel width or height, no absolute velocity, and recovery, discharge and battery limits.
steps.quote: At the current stage, we are only able to produce the planar topology of the water flow path.

steps.action: Authors conclude that the iHMM method reconstructs flow paths from inertial data with two known coordinates, even from a single deployment.
steps.quote: shows the possibility of reconstructing water flow paths from inertial data with only two given coordinates

steps.action: Referee asked for comparison with other methods (dye tracing, GPR, seismic, satellite); the final paper adds GPR and seismic-array comparisons (§4.4 ¶1, ¶3, ¶4).
steps.quote: it lacks a wider comparison with other methods (dye tracing, GPR, seismic, satellite observations)

steps.action: Referee asked authors to state the method's advantages and limitations; the final paper has a perspectives-and-limitations section (§4.4).
steps.quote: the authors highlight (1) the advantages and limitations of their method

steps.action: Referee questioned the reliability of the prototype GNSS reference drifter; the final paper discusses reference accuracy and its limits (§4.1 ¶1).
steps.quote: I would like to see much more detail about the reliability of this drifter, as well as the method in general.

steps.action: Referee asked for comparison with the GPR mapping of Church et al. at Rhonegletscher; the final paper compares length errors (§4.4 ¶1).
steps.quote: I think comparison with the work of Church et al. at the Rhonegletscher should be considered

steps.action: Referee suggested Maniatis (2021) on IMU validation in geomorphology; the final paper cites it as a general IMU validation problem (§4.4 ¶2).
steps.quote: I would also recommend looking to other disciplines for validation

steps.action: Referee asked for the glaciological significance of detecting step-pool sequences; the final paper adds their role in incision, roughness and water transit (§4.2 ¶1).
steps.quote: Essentially: we can measure step-pool sequences, so what

steps.action: Referee asked whether the supraglacial reference was checked by walkover or aerial imagery; no such check appears in the final paper (inferred decline; author response PDF not supplied).
steps.quote: did you try this for the supraglacial channel?

steps.action: Referee asked how the handheld GPS measurements were used; the final paper states they were plotted in QGIS to estimate the 85 m missing section (§4.1 ¶2).
steps.quote: it’s not clear how these measurements have been used. Are they plotted?

steps.action: Referee asked for the path length behind the required-deployment estimate; the final paper specifies at least three deployments for a 1 km channel, scaling with length (§4.3 ¶1).
steps.quote: Please be specific on the likely path length for this assessment.

steps.action: Referee noted that the conclusions introduced the gravity-vector limitation; the final paper moves it to the discussion (§4.4 ¶2).
steps.quote: there is little detail about the gravity vector problem in the main body of the results and discussion

end.claim: Submersible-drifter IMU data processed with an iHMM feature-based piecewise integration reconstruct 2D englacial flow paths between two known points (mean error 3.9 m supraglacial, 12.1 m englacial) and spatially reference water pressure.

decisive_move.sentence: The iHMM extraction of flow features, which bounds dead-reckoning error by integrating piecewise between features, is what makes the spatially referenced path possible.

gates.evidence: Deployments were designed to test the reconstruction against GNSS references (§2.2 ¶3), but no rival hypothesis directed acquisition. The reconstruction faced quantitative comparison with GNSS, satellite and GPR references (§3.1 ¶1, §3.2 ¶2) it could have failed, though no acceptance threshold was fixed. Nothing is reported as fixed before the data; filter thresholds and data clipping were set during processing (§2.4 ¶2).

imports.item: Infinite hidden Markov model with hierarchical Dirichlet process priors
Probabilistic mapping and salient-feature landmarks against dead-reckoning error
Gait-based zero-velocity resets to bound integration error (Fourati et al. 2013)
Dynamic time warping for aligning deployments
Bosch BNO055 9-DOF IMU and TE MS5837 pressure sensors

novelty_claims.quote: our method would be extendable to the reconstruction of other, previously underexplored subsurface fluid flow paths such as pipelines or karst caves
The main focus of our presented method is to provide spatial reference for measurements where such reference is currently lacking.

limits: Sub-claims at other statuses: the step-pool identification at the pressure peak is a best_explanation checked against one speleological observation and lidar; the pressure distribution and single-deployment precision (0.66 %) are estimate_with_resolution; the required number of deployments is a rough estimate. Data selection: 18 and 16 deployments reduced to 11 and 6 complete datasets (Table 1); the paper does not show whether incomplete runs differ. Filter thresholds (1σ/2σ, SD over 3) and manual outlier removal are not justified or varied. The GNSS reference is itself a prototype, and the englacial references are from other years (1999, 2020) or are satellite tracks with poor canyon visibility, so the englacial error mixes method error with channel change. The author of the 2018 speleological investigation is not stated (inference: probably the authors). The author responses are attached PDFs not supplied, so review moves are inferred by comparing the referee requests with the final text; the decline of RC2 ¶13 is inferred from absence. Composition coded capability_first because the walk builds and characterizes a method with no rivals, though the entry is framed as a problem.

disagreements.target: Hydraulic-potential concepts (Shreve 1972) as used in glacier models
disagreements.support: The paper cites others' field observations and the scarcity of direct validation; it offers no test of its own.
disagreements.quote: Direct observations to validate the connection between assumed water pressure and resulting water pathways are sparse

disagreements.target: Seismic inference and borehole/moulin measurement of water pressure
disagreements.support: The paper argues these are indirect or point-scale and offers drifter pressure along the path instead.
disagreements.quote: in the first case the measurements are not direct, and in the latter they are point scale [...]

disagreements.target: Stuart et al. (2003): pressurized flow in the Austre Brøggerbreen englacial channel
disagreements.support: Drifter pressures in 2019 show atmospheric flow, attributed to channel change since 1999.
disagreements.quote: The pressures recorded by the submersible drifters in the englacial channel show flow under atmospheric conditions.

disagreements.target: Church et al. (2020) GPR mapping of an englacial channel (2.4 % length error)
disagreements.support: The paper argues its length error scales with channel length and would be similar to GPR for shorter channels; it concedes GPR gives width and height.
disagreements.quote: This indicates that the error in our method scales with the length of the investigated channel

disagreements.target: Traditional GPR investigations (risk and time cost, Church et al. 2020, 2021)
disagreements.support: Single deployment point, about 11 min transit per drifter versus days of GPR, and direct pressure measurement.
disagreements.quote: our method also offers several advantages compared to traditional GPR investigations

alternatives_considered.chosen: Noise removal section by section after changepoint splitting
alternatives_considered.reason: Avoid over-smoothing of the remaining water flow path

alternatives_considered.reason: Removing gravity in postprocessing adds uncertainty
Error converges at six; decrease only 2.5 %
